about.title: How it works — and why your data is safe.
about.lede: LabML is a machine learning lab that runs entirely in your browser. This page explains the engine, and how each design choice keeps your data on your machine.

how.title: How it works
how.body: Your CSV is parsed in a Web Worker inside this tab. The lab profiles every column, detects the task from your target, then holds back 20% of the rows (seeded, stratified) before fitting anything — imputation, encoding and scaling are learned on the training split only, so the test score is honest. Six models train in the worker and land on a live leaderboard, always compared to a naive baseline. Insights (confusion matrix, ROC, permutation importance, what-if) interrogate the real trained models kept in worker memory.

local.title: Read locally, provably
local.body: The file never leaves the tab. Open your browser's Network panel and run a full training: no requests go out. The Content-Security-Policy of this site forbids third-party calls altogether — that is the proof, not a promise.

storage.title: History stays here
storage.body: Saved runs live in your browser's IndexedDB — metrics and charts only, never the source rows. Delete them anytime; nothing exists anywhere else.

share.title: Data-free sharing
share.body: Share links compress the run's metrics into the URL fragment — the part after # that browsers never send to any server. Your correspondent sees the results, not your data.

offline.title: Works offline
offline.body: LabML is an installable PWA: once loaded, cut the Wi-Fi and everything — demo datasets included — still works. Hard to exfiltrate data without a network.

openSource.title: Under the hood
openSource.body: The entire lab — parsing, models, metrics — is hand-written and covered by automated tests (unit, end-to-end, accessibility). No external ML service, no CDN: everything ships with the app.

home.lede: Drop a dataset, pick what to predict, and train a set of models on your own machine. No account, no upload, no setup — and every run is scored against an honest baseline.

home.statusBody: The three modules are live: the ML Lab (training, insights, export, offline PWA), AI vision (on-device image classification) and the Data Studio (quality report, cleaning, hand-off to the lab).

lab.dropTitle: Drop a CSV or Excel file
lab.dropHint: or click to browse — the file is read right here in your browser, nothing is uploaded
lab.errorBody: The file looks empty or not tabular. Try a CSV with a header row.
lab.errorTooLargeTitle: File too large for browser memory
lab.errorTooLarge: This file exceeds the {{max}}-cell budget (rows × columns) the lab holds in memory — reading stopped, on purpose, at {{rows}} rows × {{cols}} columns. Split the file or drop columns, then try again.

unsupported.type: This column cannot be a target — pick a numeric or categorical column.
unsupported.tooManyClasses: Too many distinct classes for a target — pick a column with at most 20.

lab.leakAlert: Target leakage: {{columns}} almost perfectly mirrors the target — excluded automatically.
lab.trainConfig: seed {{seed}} · split {{split}} · trained in your browser
lab.reproducibleNote: Same data, same seed, same results — every run is reproducible by construction.

leaderboard.runInfo: seed {{seed}} · {{train}} train rows · {{test}} test rows · {{features}} features after encoding
leaderboard.skipped: skipped (dates and identifiers are not features): {{columns}}
leaderboard.trainedOnTitle: Trained on an announced seeded sample of {{rows}} of the {{total}} training rows — never silently. The score comes from the same full test set as every other model.
leaderboard.sampledFrom: announced sample: {{cap}} of {{from}} usable rows (seeded, stratified)

forecast.title: Time series
forecast.hint: This dataset carries a date column. The lab can forecast a numeric value over time: naive, seasonal naive, exponential smoothing (SES, Holt, additive Holt-Winters — hand-written), the winner picked by a rolling-origin backtest that never peeks at the future.
forecast.summary: {{points}} points ({{freq}}) · backtest on the last {{holdout}} points · winner: {{winner}} with MAE {{mae}} (naive: {{naive}}).
forecast.note: The band is the empirical 80% interval of the winner's one-step backtest errors — measured, not assumed. Every method was scored on forecasts made strictly before each held-out point.

explore.title: Explore without a target
explore.hint: No column to predict? The lab can group similar rows on its own: seeded k-means (k = 2–5, chosen by silhouette) on the same encoded features, projected in 2D by PCA — hand-written, deterministic, in your browser.
explore.summary: {{k}} groups · silhouette {{silhouette}} (tried k = {{tried}}) · {{rows}} rows · the two PCA axes carry {{p1}} % + {{p2}} % of the variance
explore.note: Groups are a reading aid, not a ground truth: k-means favors roundish groups of similar size. Same data, same seed — same groups, always.

tuning.title: Hyperparameter search
tuning.hint: Seeded random search: up to {{budget}} configurations scored by {{folds}}-fold cross-validation on the training split only — the held-out test set is scored exactly once, at the end.
tuning.note: The winner is chosen by cross-validation, never by peeking at the test set — so the test delta can be negative. That is honest evaluation, not a bug.
tuning.sampled: Search ran on an announced seeded sample of {{rows}} of {{from}} training rows — the same rows the leaderboard model trained on.

batch.title: Score a new batch
batch.hint: The production gesture: drop a new file and {{model}} scores it right here — predictions for every row, and if the file carries the target column, an honest comparison against the held-out test set. Nothing is uploaded.
batch.missingColumns: This file is missing feature columns the model needs: {{list}}.
batch.error: This file could not be scored ({{detail}}).
batch.unknownLabels_one: {{count}} row carries a label never seen in training — predicted, but kept out of the metrics.
batch.unknownLabels_other: {{count}} rows carry labels never seen in training — predicted, but kept out of the metrics.
batch.noTarget: No target column in this file — predictions only, no metrics to compare.
batch.note: A drop against the test set is a signal, not a bug: the world moved. Check the input drift in the Data Studio (PSI) to see which columns shifted.

threshold.title: Decision threshold & imbalance
threshold.hint: Only {{rate}} % of rows are “{{positive}}”: accuracy flatters any model here. The precision-recall curve tells the truth, the calibration curve says whether the probabilities can be trusted — and the threshold is YOUR decision, priced by your costs.
threshold.note: A probability is not a decision. Above the threshold the row is flagged “positive” — moving it trades false alarms against missed cases, and the right trade depends on what each mistake costs YOU. The dot on the curve is your current choice; it is saved with the run.

segments.title: Where the model fails
segments.hint: The test set ({{rows}} rows) is sliced by each categorical column — including columns kept out of the features, where proxy effects can hide. Slices with fewer than {{min}} test rows are excluded.
segments.small_one: {{count}} slice with fewer than {{min}} test rows excluded.
segments.small_other: {{count}} slices with fewer than {{min}} test rows excluded.
segments.note: A gap is a finding to investigate, not a verdict — a small slice moves for one hard row as easily as for a real weakness. A gap on a column outside the features means the model reaches it through proxies.

uncertainty.title: How solid are these numbers?
uncertainty.hint: The test set ({{rows}} rows) is bootstrap-resampled and each model's {{metric}} is recomputed every time — the interval is where the metric lands 95 times out of 100. A wide interval is information, not a defect.
uncertainty.verdictReal: {{winner}} beats {{against}}: Δ {{metric}} = {{delta}} [{{lo}} ; {{hi}}] — the gap survives resampling ({{share}}% of resamples). Probably real.
uncertainty.verdictNoise: {{winner}} vs {{against}}: Δ {{metric}} = {{delta}} [{{lo}} ; {{hi}}] — the interval crosses zero. Possibly noise: on this test set, the winner is not proven better.
uncertainty.note: Resamples are drawn from the same {{rows}} test rows (seed {{seed}}, shared across models so comparisons are paired). These intervals measure sensitivity to the test draw — not training variance.

compare.title: Run comparison
compare.notComparable: These runs predict different things — the metrics do not compare. The configuration diff below still tells the story.
compare.read: The best model goes from {{aPrimary}} ({{aModel}}) to {{bPrimary}} ({{bModel}}) — {{metric}} {{delta}}.
compare.sameFeatures: Both runs trained on the same features.
compare.intervalsDisjoint: The intervals do not overlap — the gap between the two runs exceeds both uncertainties. Probably real.
compare.intervalsOverlap: The intervals overlap — on these test sets, the gap between the two runs could be noise.
compare.intervalsNote: Each interval comes from its own run's test draw (v20). Two runs are never paired — read this as an indication, not a test.

imported.title: Reuse an exported model
imported.hint: Trained here before? Drop the exported model (.json) — it scores new files without retraining. Everything stays in your browser.
imported.scoreCta: Score a CSV with this model
imported.scoreHint: The file must carry the feature columns above; a target column is optional and only feeds the honest comparison.
imported.note: The reference column is the exporting run's held-out test — a different draw than this file. Read gaps as signals, not verdicts.

insights.title: Insights
insights.selectHint: Click any leaderboard row to inspect another model.
insights.importanceHintClassification: Accuracy drop when the column is shuffled (permutation importance, model-agnostic).
insights.importanceHintRegression: RMSE increase when the column is shuffled (permutation importance, model-agnostic).
insights.readAccuracy: {{model}} gets {{accuracy}}% of the {{rows}} held-out test rows right.
insights.readBaseline: That is {{delta}} points above the naive baseline ({{baseline}}%), so the model has learned real signal.
insights.readRecall: It catches {{recall}}% of the actual "{{label}}" cases.
insights.readRegression: {{model}}'s predictions are off by {{mae}} on average across the {{rows}} held-out test rows.
insights.readVariance: It explains {{r2}}% of the variance of the target.
insights.pdpHint: Average model prediction as this column sweeps its range, everything else unchanged.
insights.whatIfHint: Edit the values and watch the model's live prediction — computed locally, like everything else.
insights.explainTitle: What pushes the value up or down, versus a typical row
insights.explainTitleClass: What pushes toward or away from “{{class}}”, versus a typical row
insights.explainNote: Shapley values estimated by permutation sampling ({{permutations}} permutations × {{references}} reference rows, seeded). The bars sum exactly to the gap between this prediction and the reference average.
insights.wordsHintClassification: Average shift of the predicted probability of “{{class}}” when the word is erased from the reviews containing it — right pushes up, left pushes down.
insights.wordsHintRegression: Average shift of the prediction when the word is erased from the texts containing it — right pushes up, left pushes down.
insights.wordsNote: One word at a time, on the held-out test rows. A review says the same thing several ways, so erasing one word rarely flips a prediction on its own.

export.knnNote: k-NN cannot be exported — it memorizes the training data.

data.title: Diagnose and clean a dataset, without uploading it.
data.lede: Drop a file: the studio measures its quality — missing values, duplicates, inconsistent spellings, outliers — then repairs it with a transparent recipe. Entirely in your browser, like the rest of LabML.

drop.title: Drop a CSV or Excel file
drop.hint: or click to browse — .csv, .tsv, .xlsx. Read locally in a Web Worker, never uploaded.

data.error: This file could not be read ({{detail}}). Try a CSV, TSV or Excel file with a header row.

join.title: Join a second file
join.hint: Enrich {{name}} with columns from another file, matched on a shared key column. Matching is exact after trimming — a messy key shows up as an orphan, not silently. The joined result becomes THE dataset: quality report, recipe, drift and the ML Lab all continue from it.
join.noKey: No column name in common between the two files — the key must exist on both sides.
join.verdict: {{other}} joined on “{{key}}”: {{matched}} of {{total}} rows matched, {{columns}} columns added.
join.orphans_one: {{count}} row found no match — unmatched key: {{keys}}.
join.orphans_other: {{count}} rows found no match — unmatched keys: {{keys}}.
join.duplicates_one: {{count}} duplicated key on the joined file (first occurrence wins).
join.duplicates_other: {{count}} duplicated keys on the joined file (first occurrence wins).
join.unused_one: {{count}} row of the joined file matched nothing.
join.unused_other: {{count}} rows of the joined file matched nothing.
join.note: Left join: every original row survives; unmatched rows keep empty new columns. Orphans caused by messy keys (case, spaces) are a cleaning finding — merge the variants in the recipe below.

issues.title: What the studio found
issues.none: Nothing to report: no missing cells, duplicates, spelling variants or outliers. This dataset is ready.

missing.body: Empty cells and tokens like “NA” or “?”. Models cannot use them as-is: fill them or drop the rows.

duplicates.body: Rows identical to an earlier row. They double-count observations and can leak between train and test splits.

messy.body: The same category written several ways (case, stray spaces). Left as-is, each spelling counts as a different category.

outliers.body: Values outside the Tukey fences (1.5 × IQR) of their column — often typos or unit mix-ups. Check before clamping.

structural.body: Constant or near-empty columns carry no signal; identifiers are flagged for information and never dropped automatically.

recipe.title: Cleaning recipe
recipe.importError: This file is not a LabML recipe.
recipe.typesHint: Force how a column is treated by the cleaning steps (variant merging, imputation, outlier clamping, date expansion). “Auto” keeps the inferred type.

toggles.mergeVariants: Merge spelling variants to the most frequent form
toggles.clipOutliers: Clamp outliers to the Tukey fences

preview.title: Preview
preview.note_one: First row shown — missing cells appear as “—”.
preview.note_other: First {{count}} rows shown — missing cells appear as “—”.

drift.title: Drift check
drift.hint: Compare a new batch against {{name}} (the loaded reference): schema differences, distribution shifts (PSI), new or vanished categories. The new file is parsed in your browser too — nothing is uploaded.
drift.verdict: {{name}} vs the reference: {{drifted}} of {{total}} columns drifted ({{refRows}} → {{newRows}} rows).
drift.note: PSI (Population Stability Index) measures how much a column’s distribution moved, over bins built from the reference. Conventional reading: < 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate, > 0.25 strong — a model trained on the reference should be re-examined.

privacy.title: Nothing leaves your browser
privacy.body: The file is parsed and cleaned inside a Web Worker; the page only ever receives the quality report, counters and a few preview rows. Exports are generated locally, and “Open in the ML Lab” hands the cleaned dataset to the lab in memory — no server is involved at any point, as the strict Content-Security-Policy of this site enforces.

ai.title: Deep learning, still in your browser.
ai.lede: Neural modules built on the same rule as the lab: the model comes to your data — never the other way around.

vision.title: Vision playground
vision.description: Classify a photo, find every object and locate faces with three real neural networks on ONNX Runtime Web — running in a Web Worker on your machine.

chat.title: Chat over your data
chat.description: Ask questions in plain French or English — averages, counts with conditions, top N, correlations. A deterministic local interpreter, not a language model: your data and your questions never leave the browser.

chat.title: Ask your data a question.
chat.lede: Load a dataset and ask in plain French or English: averages, medians, counts under a condition, top N, breakdowns, correlations, missing values. Everything is interpreted and computed right here.

drop.title: Drop a CSV or Excel file
drop.hint: or click to browse — read locally in a Web Worker, never uploaded.

chat.error: This file could not be read. Try a CSV, TSV or Excel file with a header row.
chat.welcome: Ready. Ask a question below, or tap one of the ideas.

answers.correlation: Pearson correlation between {{a}} and {{b}}: {{value}} over {{rows}} pairs — {{strength}}.

strength.weak: a weak or no linear link

answers.noMissing: No missing cells — this dataset is complete.

chat.unknown: I did not understand that. I am a deterministic interpreter, not a language model: ask for an average, a median, a min/max, a sum, a count under a condition, a top N, a breakdown, a correlation or the missing values — naming your columns.

honesty.title: Honest by design
honesty.body: This assistant is a deterministic local interpreter — not a language model. It only computes what it fully understands, says so when it does not, and neither your data nor your questions ever leave the browser. A generative assistant would need a model behind an API — a server and a secret key that must never ship in a browser — and would only land here with a server-side proxy and an explicit consent screen.
honesty.coming: Coming soon: a real language model — small, open and running entirely in your browser, under the same privacy rules. The deterministic interpreter stays as the honest fallback.

vision.title: What does a neural network see?
vision.lede: Drop a photo: three self-hosted neural networks — an EfficientNet-Lite4 classifier (1,000 classes), a YOLOX-Nano object detector (80 kinds of things) and an UltraFace face detector — run locally through ONNX Runtime Web (WebAssembly). The image never leaves your browser.
vision.loading: Downloading the three models (~19 MB, once — they are then cached, offline included)…
vision.error: The model could not be loaded or run. Reload the page and check your connection for the first download.

drop.title: Drop an image here
drop.hint: or click to browse — JPEG, PNG, WebP… It is processed locally, nothing is uploaded.

webcam.error: Camera unavailable or permission denied — the file drop above still works.

results.title: What the networks see
results.working: The network is looking at your image…
results.empty: The analysis will appear here once you drop an image.
results.note: EfficientNet-Lite4 (77.6 % ImageNet top-1) still always answers with its closest of 1,000 classes — even on an image it does not understand — and its class names stay in English.
results.subject: Main subject — ImageNet top 5
results.objectsNone: No objects detected — nothing above the 35 % confidence bar.
results.detNote: Detection says where, not who: YOLOX-Nano knows the 80 everyday COCO classes (35 % confidence bar), UltraFace only locates faces — neither recognizes anyone, and nothing leaves the tab.

how.title: How it works — and why it is private
how.body: The photo is prepared in canvases (a 224² center crop, a 416² letterbox and a 320×240 frame), then handed to a Web Worker where ONNX Runtime executes the three networks in WebAssembly; the box math — grids, IoU, non-maximum suppression — is hand-written and unit-tested. Models and runtime are served by this site itself: the strict Content-Security-Policy still forbids any third-party call, so the photo cannot leave the tab.
